title: Emptiness, Liberation, and Beauty, with Rob Burbea

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for modern mutants interested in mindfulness, meditation, awakening, hardcore dharma, consciousness hacking, emptiness, and more.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast. And in this episode, I'm speaking with Rob Burbea.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Rob Burbea is a meditation teacher, musician, and author who teaches at Gaia House in Devon, England.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Rob is the author of the groundbreaking meditation practice book entitled Seeing That Frees, Meditations on Emptiness and Dependent Arising.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I personally love this book and I recommend it to anyone who really wants to investigate the deeper ends of meditation practice. And Rob and I will discuss the book and the practices in the book in depth in this episode.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And now, without further ado, I give you the episode that I call Emptiness, Liberation, and Beauty with Rob Burbea.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Rob, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Thank you, Michael. Pleasure to be here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's a real pleasure for me. I've been a big fan of your book, Seeing That Frees, and so it's just a total delight to get to speak with you live here.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So, as I mentioned, the name of your book is Seeing That Frees. When you think about it, it's a somewhat unusual name. Often when I'm talking to another person and I'm like recommending it, I say, I just love this book, Seeing That Frees. And they're like, what? Freeze? Like ice or seeing? What are you saying? And I have to repeat it several times and I end up saying something to say it in a different way, like looking that liberates or ways of looking that cause us to be free. You get it? Seeing That Frees.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And then they're like, "Oh, okay, okay."

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: But the more I've been asked to kind of explain the title, it's almost been a little bit of a mindfulness exercise in just thinking about the meaning of that title, Seeing That Frees. It's quite a compelling phrase. And so I just want to begin with that very simple fact of the title of the book and the idea of ways of seeing that could actually be liberating to human beings. And I'd just like to hear your intention for the title and what that means to you,

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: seeing that is liberating.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Yes, I'm aware some people really don't like the title and don't get it, and some people love it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I definitely am among those who love it.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: I hear that. So, in a way, there's a double meaning in the title, and oftentimes with titles of talks and different things, I like to play with double or even triple meanings just to cram a lot in there. But we can come back to that. As you point out, there's actually one way you could look at the way the book works or what it presents and what it takes for a ride. There's two central kind of concepts or strands.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: And one is, as you say, ways of looking or ways of seeing, if you like. I actually usually prefer the word looking because it implies a little bit more intentionality than seeing, which we tend to associate with a bit more passivity. So one concept is ways of looking and the other is fabrication. And so we could say, as you said, ways of looking that liberate would mean it would encapsulate at least one of the meanings in the title. And what this really refers to is that as human beings, we have this amazing capacity

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: to look at things in different ways. But by look at, I actually mean sense things in different ways or relate to things in different ways or conceive in different ways. So all of that is packed into this idea of ways of looking. It's the totality of what's involved in any moment of perceiving anything whatsoever that comprises my reactions, subtle or gross, my preconceptions, my ideation, my likes and dislikes,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: and dislikes, the kind of mode of viewing with which I'm looking at. So all that comprises the way of looking at any moment. And the book just starts with the premise that, well, you know what, as human beings, we have this capacity, as I said, to look in different ways, to experience in different ways. Deliberately, we can change our ways of looking at things. So, you know, a classic one from the Dharma would be, and I'm just pulling this out of

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: infinite number of possibilities. A classic one in the Dharma would be just to see something that's going on, let's say my body sensations right now, or even the thoughts that I'm having as I'm speaking this, and to regard them as not me, not mine. This is a classical anatta way of looking, as I would call it. That's a mode of looking. Typical, more, let's say, normal human way of looking would be to regard them as mine. These are my sensations.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: I am this mind or whatever. So that's just an example of two contrasting ways of looking. The premise of the book is, or one of the premises of the book, is that humans have this capacity to explore deliberately developing, let's say, skills or arts of lots of different ways of looking and experimenting with them and finding out what they do. Because, for instance, if I'm sitting here and I have a pain in my back right now and I see it as,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: not-self, or if I'm thinking, well, maybe Michael thinks I'm stupid and I'm not making sense, and my mind isn't as sharp as Michael's, or whatever, and I'm identifying with my mind, if I view it as not-self, then any kind of, or to a large degree, to a very profound degree, the suffering that's associated with that identification with the mind, or the identification with these being my sensations of pain or whatever, that goes. So we see that one way of looking in this example,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: liberates, it frees. It's a kind of seeing that frees. And the other, relatively speaking, causes in Dharma language more contraction, more pain.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: More than that, though, we see that if I really start practicing this, let's take that as an example because I started with it, that way of looking, not me, not mine, it doesn't just stop there, bringing a momentary release of suffering. I actually start to see if I really practice it and I get quite skilled at it and develop it over a range of different objects of my experience. Then I notice other things. The sense of self starts to change. In other words, this way of looking,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: starts to affect not just the dukkha, the experience suffering in the moment, but also the sense of self, the experience of self in the moment. That becomes, for example, less solid, less separate, more spacious, etc., lighter through that way of looking. And if I take it even further, I find that with that same way of looking, this anatta way of looking, the very perception of the world starts to change. Certainly these objects themselves, of course they're seen as not me, not mine,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: But that perception of objects itself starts to, in the language of the book, the other central premises, it's fabricated less. They start to appear less solid. Not just that they're kind of unhooked from my identification, unhooked from belonging to me or being me, but they actually, with practice, over time, they start to feel less solid, less substantial. It's almost like they're less intense as experiences. We say they're fabricated less. Those perceptions are fabricated less.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: And that lessening of fabrication moves along a spectrum with the development of my skill in that way of looking. And in some instances can go all the way to those sensations, et cetera, not appearing at all. They're not fabricated at all. So this is just one example. We learn through that way of looking, it's a particularly powerful one, through that way of looking, it's not just a kind of neat trick to reduce suffering in the moment. It starts telling me something about what is perceived

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: what appears to us, what we experience with different ways of looking. So I start experimenting playing with different ways of looking. As I said, there are infinite amounts. And in the paradigm of a kind of movement towards liberation, I'm particularly interested in that experimenting, in that playing. Not just with gaining skill, but with really noticing what are the effects of this way of looking on my sense of self, on the dukkha, on the sense of things.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: effects of that way of looking on the dukkha, on the sense of self, on the sense of things. And so it becomes this journey of exploration with these twin kind of entwined concepts of ways of looking and fabrication. Fabrication refers to the other central strand of concept, really refers to how does my way of looking give rise to this experience or this sense of things or this suffering. So we say dukkha, suffering, dis-ease is fabricated

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: a large extent by my way of looking and similarly the sense of self and similarly the sense of things.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: And so it's taking those really basic concepts that are sort of, I would say, hard to argue with, that human beings can play with their ways of looking, and that we can see, even at a gross level, that the way of looking fabricates, to some extent, what we perceive.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So I see that when I'm completely crazy, what Buddhists call papañca, and my mind is just running riot with all this kind of story making and nonsense. But in that experience, I fabricate a whole sense of self, certainly quite a lot of suffering, usually, and a kind of world involving certain very prominent objects and a whole tangled solidity of perception. And then when we come out of that kind of craziness, that way of looking, which wasn't an intentional way of looking,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: that papañca then we see oh it was a fabrication

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So take these two concepts, ways of looking at fabrication, which I would say are kind of obvious to a certain extent. A little bit of self-awareness just reveals those possibilities. And we say, what if we don't close them down or limit them as concepts? And what if we just open them up as sort of avenues of exploration? In other words, what ways of looking are possible without limiting how many are legitimate and not pre-assuming what is fabricated and what isn't?

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: example at a very gross level. I can see when I'm in this state of catastrophizing sort of semi-hysteria, whatever, that we call papañca. It's a very gross state. I come out of it, a little time goes by, I come out of it, I feel better, I see things differently. I look back, I say, oh, that was fabricated, all that nonsense. Look what a crazy world I made up and crazy self-views I had. And so we say that was fabricated. But in the back of my mind, I may be thinking that was fabricated, but this desk that I'm sitting at or this microphone or this conversation or whatever,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: that's all real, that's not fabricated. What if we just don't rush in so quickly with the typical assumptions of what is fabricated and what is not fabricated? Where is the limit of fabrication? Let's not impose that from the beginning. Together with that exploration of fabrication, we also explore it through this gradually developing of playing with different ways of looking, and we see how they affect each other. And that brings not just liberation in the moment,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: understanding about the dependent arising of suffering, of the sense of self, and of the sense of anything whatsoever, any phenomenon whatsoever. And that explains the subtitle of the book, Meditations on Emptiness and Dependent Arising. So in Buddhist teachings, when something is a dependent arising, it means it's empty. It has no independent existence, no inherent existence.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: And the premise of the book is we can really have a lot of joy and fun playing with these explorations. And usually gradually with a kind of quantum leaps or whatever, it's a bit little and unpredictable, but there comes not just the joy of playing with it, not just the temporary relief of suffering, but there comes a kind of radically deep insights overturning our usual assumptions about what is real, what is not real, what is this self, what is this world, what is a thing.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: What is awareness? What is time? What is space? Etc, etc. So that's the kind of the way the book works. But I also, I think, mentioned before that the title has potentially a double meaning with the emphasis on the that. So seeing that frees. The that being what? Being either the unfabricated, the deathless, or emptiness. So that's there. That meaning is there as well. But in a way, the way I would conceive of the whole thing is that the freedom that's possible is even,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: even deeper and wider than seeing the unfabricated, seeing the deathless. So the sort of primary title is more, as you kind of interpreted it yourself earlier, Michael, Seeing That Frees, Ways of Looking That Liberate. What the book unfolds is that in the end, what we're left with is just this range of ways of looking and this kind of possibility of play and art to conjure, to weave different experiences, different senses of self,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: world, knowing that it's all empty. Because it's all empty, we have that freedom. So that goes beyond even a particular kind of seeing, seeing that frees.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: I'm just curious, of course, you know, these ideas and these experiences of emptiness and dependent origination are at the core of Buddhist practice, and yet you seem to have made a rather thorough investigation of this, and in kind of an unusual way. I want to unpack that just a little bit, what I mean by unusual, and that is that you seem to have come at it from many, many different directions, with many different types of meditations,

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: is not that typical and quite interesting and have documented this very clearly in the book, Seeing That Frees. So my curiosity here is how you began working in this very, like I would say, creative way that is, I think, so intriguing about your work. It's very creative. It's clear that you're devising new exercises or modifying or updating classical techniques and that there's just this

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: mode of absolute investigative wonder and curiosity about it. And there's no feeling that you're trying to like get from stage X to stage Y or whatever, but instead really just experimenting and having openness. And I really appreciate that mood. And I'm wondering if you can share with us how you began that investigation and how it unfolded for you in such a deep and rich manner that you've documented in the book.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Interesting question, Michael. My immediate response is I can't remember, but I'm sure it'll come to me in a minute. My other immediate response is, so if there's a story, then this will be like today's version of the story, which might be a different, you know, telling of history on another day or in another mood or whatever. Yes. You know, past is empty too. So I know where I got the idea of fabrication from. I got that from Ajahn Thanissaro, who maybe many of your listeners will know him.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Ajahn Geoff, who is an American monk, but abbot of a monastery in San Diego. He was a monk in Thailand for 25 years or more, I think. He was a very important teacher for me for a kind of short period. I was actually thinking of becoming a monk at his monastery for a while. The idea of fabrication I got from him, I'm not sure if he would feel, if he read Seeing That Frees, whether he felt I had taken it too far and beyond the range of what he would feel comfortable with or into territory that he would

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: not feel calm, I don't know. But I remember getting the idea of that from him, and it's a certain translation of the word saṅkhāra, fabrication. The experiment thing, I think...

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: I don't know, maybe it's just a kind of personality type I have. I was a jazz musician for a long time. That was my work before I was a full-time Dharma bum. And I think that kind of idea of improvising and being creative and trying things out is just kind of my type, maybe, to a certain extent.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: You know, I spent some time in meditation just running into brick walls and then trying different things and then those walls opening or disappearing or whatever and avenues opening up. So I think I learned, you know, from difficult experience. It's a curious thing with this way of approaching things that I outline in the book is that the very approach of playing with ways of looking turns out to be in a way the goal as well.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: the emptiness of awareness, the emptiness of time, the emptiness of the present moment, the emptiness of everything, the unfabricated, the deathless, all the way through that. And we emerge with just this kind of full permission of the beauty of free play with ways of looking to serve different purposes, of which the paradigmatic one in Buddha Dharma is the purpose of relieving suffering and increasing compassion.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So in some sense, the premise of the book, or one of the premises, one of the sort of starting strands of the book, turns out to be the actual delivery point where it all ends up. So that's part of it. I think maybe another sort of weave in the story was, and again, it's today's story right now at this time when you're asking me, I think perhaps I certainly felt helped by a lot of the teachings that were out there. Certainly, as mentioned, I've known Jeff and Christopher Titmuss and Christina Feldman.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: actually lots of teachings. But I also felt somehow nothing kind of fully satisfied me. There were lots of questions that I couldn't really find answers to, or people with the same degree of burning interest in them. And so I had a lot of time on retreat, years in fact, and I was, to a certain extent, it was a natural kind of move for me to just begin experimenting.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: and seeing what happened and getting super interested in this stuff and with this kind of burning curiosity about it all.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And can you actually remember that moment of kind of leaving the well-worn trail and going off into, just to horribly mix metaphors for a moment, going off into your jazz improv on emptiness?

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Probably not, but I remember I had this question for a while about the nature of awareness.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: and I was just struck by, again, how unsatisfactory I found the answers about the relationship of awareness and the deathless and the unfabricated, etc. There were a lot of different answers, all of which I felt, for me at that time, were not satisfactory.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: And what I also encountered in some of the people I talked to was just

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: it was clear that it wasn't really an interesting question to them. Or that level of meditative territory or inquiry or that level of liberation just wasn't that interesting. And I think it was more that those signals of lack of interest and also the absence of answers that were satisfying that kind of made me just tip ever so slightly off an edge that I was already kind of on already, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: That's the story that comes out now that you ask me.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, it is interesting when many times when I've asked teachers about emptiness or heard teachers respond to questions about emptiness, they'll give kind of a pat answer out of the Questions of King Menander, you know, like, well, there's a chariot and you take it apart and it's no longer a chariot and you put it back together and it's a chariot.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: you know, that's about it. In every other way, it's too deep to talk about and too deep to understand. Not to be too critical here, but it seems like there's almost like an abdication of the possibility of talking about it or describing practices that will actually give you more insight into emptiness in a very direct way. For some reason, that's either taboo or not available, or as you said, just seems like they're not interested in it. So I just love that you took

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: upon yourself to just go there anyway and investigate it deeply. So besides Thanissaro Bhikkhu, what other resources did you find that helped you to do this long process of investigation into emptiness?

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So the teachings of Christopher Titmuss were really pivotal for me. Those teachings were huge. And I didn't have much personal contact with him at all. I sat a couple of retreats, I think, over a few years. But I listened to a lot of his recordings. So he has, and I think you know him, I think you even had an interview with him recently. But he has, yeah, what came through of the beauty of the promise of emptiness communicated to my soul and my heart. I love that. But also certain kind of radical insights about dependence.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: that really struck me and were really helpful for me kind of back in the mid-90s. I worked for a long time on retreat with Christina Feldman and that was very helpful as well. And then I was at Gaia House on these long retreats. The library there is very eclectic. It's not huge, but it's a fairly substantial library and it's very eclectic. So I would pick up books and, for instance, the books in the Tibetan Gelug tradition,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: to go into the realization of emptiness and at first it just left me cold and I had no resonance with it whatsoever. At what point that for instance started to come alive for me I actually don't remember and I don't remember what even prompted me to start playing with it because I was so kind of turned off by it for a long time. So I think partly in the process of working with these things and trying things out and really just following the lead of the beauty of it and the sense of the liberation at different

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: degrees of depth. It's kind of like what opened up at one depth or in one territory then made another door available, if you like, and I could walk through that one or it became interesting or it became possible. So things kind of, you know, built on each other to a certain extent. Because I was a little bit exposed to different streams of teaching, I also wanted to know how they related to each other or were they just contradictory, etc.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: But I think there's different elements that come together. One is the sort of basic overarching concept of the whole path and method and what we're doing, this idea of two strands of ways of looking and fabrication that I outlined. I don't quite remember when that really got clear, but it was fairly early. And just having that kind of conceptual framework of what practice was doing, and not just emptiness practice, any practice,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: fit into a context. It contextualized everything else. And I can remember certain periods where insights just took these quantum leaps to another level of depth. And they were really exciting times. But exactly what stimulated them, I can't remember. I remember reading Gampopa, a Tibetan teacher from, I think, the 12th century. He has a book that's usually translated as something like the Jewel Ornament of Liberation or something like that in English.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: a few lines in there about the emptiness, if I remember, of atoms and the emptiness of time. And they weren't really meditative instructions, but somehow, and again, I can't quite remember how, somehow I took these teachings, which one could just read and sort of say, okay, that sounds cool. Somehow I took it and I found ways of turning them into meditations that for me were very, very powerful. And so a lot of that kind of stuff found its way into Seeing That Frees. And I was just kind of obsessed about the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: I think that's fair to say I was pretty obsessed for a number of years about emptiness and the unfabricated and the deathless. And I had an intuition even before I got into deep practice. This drew me. I didn't quite know what it was, but I had this mystical intuition of something that was, I remember saying to someone, I would stake my life on this. I don't know what it is yet, but I just, I know that I would stake my life on it. And so that kind of intuition was there for me. And so these are some of the factors,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: I feel I'm not giving you a very good answer to your question. So that's what I can do for right now. It's today's answer,

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: which is perfect. So I'm just going to ask you an impossible question, which is, okay, Rob, you have this deep insight into emptiness. What can you say about emptiness? What is it? Why does it matter? Why should someone care?

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: At this point in my journey and my journey as a teacher, I've kind of stopped trying to convince anyone that they should care about this. I think some people will be interested even when they don't understand. I was saying to a group the other day, you know, some people hear the Heart Sutra or something like that and they know they don't understand, but they're attracted.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: something just ignites in the consciousness and they want to go towards that. They want to open up that understanding in the broad sense of the word understanding. And I think other people maybe won't ever be, you know, and even some people who are committed Dharma practitioners, they're just not going to be. And I feel that's fine. I wouldn't even judge that. I'm not interested in converting anyone to anything. There were times when I did feel more fired up and said, this is how we need to understand

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Buddhist teachings, or this is much more helpful, this will go deeper, this will make sense of everything. I just feel less inclined to do that right now. But having said all that, what is emptiness? As you said, it's an impossible question, because I find the way I speak or what I might say is very much dependent on my sense of who I'm talking to, whether I speak more poetically or more to exhort people or more logically or more polemically or whatever. And this feels like a bit of a blank right now.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: that you ask me in terms of who's listening and what kind of personalities they are and what speaks to them.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, just use me as the argument. I'm asking you.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: What is emptiness? Emptiness is...

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: something that we realize absolutely everything has as an attribute, if you like, and that realization liberates us. It opens up a radical sense of freedom in relation to everything in existence, absolutely everything. And I would say more than that, it opens up a degree of mystery and beauty in the sense of what everything is and who am I and what consciousness is

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: is.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So usually emptiness is presented in purely in the context of liberative aims, you know, for freedom, for the ending of suffering, for at least reducing suffering. And I think that's obviously really key. And the book Seeing That Frees is written in that language, in that premise. But I think it's also true that there is, for me, something sacred about the realization of emptiness. There's a sense of sacredness when we open to it. There's a sense of mystery and a sense of beauty, as well as relief and release of suffering.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So in technical language, you can say emptiness is the realization that nothing whatsoever, nothing has any what we call inherent existence, any independent existence.

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: Sometimes people translate that as meaning everything is dependent on conditions in the world. So this tree is dependent on water and sunlight and minerals from the soil and all that. And that's one interpretation of dependent arising and emptiness. But for me, the more radical, deeper, thorough, certainly more liberative and much more beautiful levels of emptiness realization come in when you include the dependence on the mind, the dependence on the ways of looking. And one starts to explore,

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: was outlining earlier, this question of how the ways of looking either fabricate more or less or differently, and that binds it, so to speak, in unbinding the mind and the self and consciousness. It also curiously binds it, connects it with the world of things and the cosmos that we experience. So there's liberation and mystery in the seeing of that lack of inherent existence. Nothing, not anything exists independent of the way

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: of looking and ways of looking too are empty everything everything

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: So for me, seeing emptiness is something that brings...

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: this really radical sense of freedom in relation to our existence, but also a lot of profound beauty, sacredness, love, all of that.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, when you talk about this lack of inherent existence, there's at least two ways we can kind of approach that.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: One is kind of a semi-scientific third-person external viewpoint like, well, things are constructed of other things and those are made of atoms and atoms are made of quarks and so on, subatomic particles and then quarks. And that's one way of conceptually approaching that. Another way of conceptually approaching it would be more first-person experiential of like actually, you know, experiencing what I would call the construction or you call the fabrication

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: of all the sensory streams and experience. Like you can just observe them being fabricated and then coming together, weaving together to then construct objects and the world and ideas and so on. There's this kind of first person seeing of the lack of inherent existence 'cause you observe it being constructed. And I'm dividing those two things 'cause one is in my mind more experiential

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: about the world.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Now, would you say your understanding of emptiness includes both of those or one or the other of those or something completely different than that?

transcript.speaker: Rob Burbea
transcript.text: If I'm understanding you, Michael, yeah, I would say for me, it includes both of those. Although in the first one that you outlined, I wouldn't stop. See, what usually happens is people engage in some degree of deconstruction and some degree of deconstruction any human being is going to agree on.
